meta.title: Who really said "And God said, Love your enemy, and I obeyed Him and loved myself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The popular “God said” version is a misquote. Gibran actually wrote “My enemy said to me, Love your enemy” — in Spiritual Sayings (1962).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'And God said, Love your enemy, and I obeyed Him and loved myself'?
meta.ogDescription: The “God said” version is a misquote. Gibran wrote “My enemy said to me, Love your enemy…” in Spiritual Sayings (1962).

answer.label: Not Gibran’s wording — a misquote of his line
answer.authorDates: 1883–1931 · Lebanese-American poet, artist & author of The Prophet
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Gibran’s, but the popular wording is altered. His actual aphorism reads “My enemy said to me, ‘Love your enemy.’ And I obeyed him and loved myself” — the sting is that it is the enemy, not God, who gives the command. Wikiquote files the “And God said…” version under Misattributed as a paraphrase of that line, and it traces to the 1962 Ferris translation in Spiritual Sayings of Kahlil Gibran.

author.kicker: The true author of the thought
author.heading: Kahlil Gibran
author.metaLine: 1883–1931 · Lebanese-American poet, artist & author of The Prophet
author.bio: Kahlil Gibran was a Lebanese-American writer and painter, best known for The Prophet (1923). He wrote in both English and Arabic, and his aphorisms — terse, paradoxical one-liners — are among the most quoted (and most rewritten) lines online. This saying about loving one’s enemy is authentically his in substance, but the widely shared “God said” wording is a later alteration.

misattribution.heading: A real Gibran line, quietly rewritten
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fabrication out of thin air — it is a genuine Gibran aphorism whose wording got changed as it spread. The change matters.

items.why: The version pinned to Gibran across social media and quote sites has God issue the command. Wikiquote lists exactly this form under its Misattributed heading, describing it as a paraphrase of Gibran’s actual line.

items.who: “My enemy said to me, ‘Love your enemy.’ And I obeyed him and loved myself.”
items.why: In the real aphorism it is the enemy who says “love your enemy” — and obeying means loving oneself. Swapping God for the enemy removes the irony that gives the line its bite. Sourced to Spiritual Sayings of Kahlil Gibran (Ferris trans., 1962).

misattribution.truthLine: Gibran wrote it — but as “My enemy said to me, ‘Love your enemy,’” not “God said.” See the sourced vs. misattributed entries on Wikiquote.

context.heading: Why the two words matter
lead: Gibran’s aphorism is a small trap. The command “love your enemy” comes from the enemy’s own mouth — so to obey it literally is to love the person the enemy is telling you to love, which (in the twist) turns out to be yourself. It is a joke about self-love smuggled inside a piece of scripture-sounding advice.

Replace “my enemy” with “God” and the irony collapses: you get a sincere-sounding endorsement of self-care instead of Gibran’s sly paradox. That is why the rewrite spread so well on feel-good quote graphics — and why it is no longer quite what Gibran wrote.
context.pull: In the real line it is the enemy, not God, who says “love your enemy.”
